<card_meaning symbol="2♦">
The Financial Partner

You name the exchange out loud and keep it fair for both sides. You understand value exchange and partnership in material terms. You're good at splitting bills, sharing assets, creating fair deals. Your mind works in reciprocity.

Balanced: You name the exchange out loud and keep it fair for both sides.

Under-expressed: You give the better end of the deal so no one can call you greedy. The short end becomes a habit, then a grudge.

Over-expressed: You steer the money so you stay in control of the relationship.

Shadow: You give the better end of the deal to keep the partnership. The short end becomes a habit, then a grudge.

Gifts: Natural understanding of fair exchange; Ability to create balanced partnerships around resources; Diplomatic skill in financial negotiations; Talent for making partnerships feel equitable

Life direction: Your curriculum is learning that true partnership requires equal contribution, not equal sacrifice. You're learning to ask for what you need materially.
</card_meaning>

<source_text>
Clarence McKay "Ace" Parker was an American football and baseball player and coach. He played professional football as a quarterback, tailback and safety in the National Football League (NFL) for the Brooklyn Dodgers (1937–1941) and the Boston Yanks (1945) and in the All-America Football Conference (AAFC) for the New York Yankees. He was an All-American selection at Duke University in 1936. Parker also played in the Major League Baseball (MLB) during 1936 and 1937 with the Philadelphia Athletics. He served as the head baseball coach at Duke from 1953 to 1966. Parker was inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame as a player in 1955 and the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1972.
</source_text>

<card_meaning symbol="J♣">
The Creative Messenger

You bring a new angle and stay long enough for someone to test it. You bring new thinking and inspiration. You're the one who shifts how people think about things. You have the gift of the "aha moment."

Balanced: You bring a new angle and you let someone pressure-test it before it ships.

Under-expressed: The idea comes out half-built. Speed stands in for a check against reality.

Over-expressed: You pitch before you have checked whether it can live. Excitement outruns the work.

Shadow: You drop the insight and leave. The shift happens; the integration does not, because you are already gone.

Gifts: Ability to inspire intellectual breakthroughs; Creative and unconventional perspective; Natural gift for shifting paradigms; Talent for generating excitement about ideas

Life direction: Your curriculum is learning that real change requires staying present. You're learning follow-through, not just catalysis.
</card_meaning>

<source_text>
Aeneas Demetrius Williams is an American former professional football player who was a cornerback and safety in the National Football League (NFL) for 14 seasons. He played college football for the Southern Jaguars and was selected in the third round of the 1991 NFL draft by the Phoenix Cardinals, where he spent 10 seasons. During his final four seasons, he was a member of the St. Louis Rams. Williams received eight Pro Bowl selections and three first-team All-Pro honors, as well as being on the second NFL 1990s All-Decade Team. He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2014.
</source_text>

<card_meaning symbol="J♦">
The Successful Messenger

You try a new approach to value and you finish enough of it to know if it works. You bring new ways of thinking about resources and success. You're the one who shifts how people relate to money. You inspire financial breakthroughs.

Balanced: You try a new approach to value and you finish enough of it to know if it works.

Under-expressed: You get excited about the next way to make money and do not stay for the unglamorous middle.

Over-expressed: You promise a return you have not built. The pitch outruns the product.

Shadow: You talk about value more fluently than you keep it. The message is ahead of the books.

Gifts: Ability to inspire financial awakening; Natural gift for shifting money mindsets; Talent for creating excitement about opportunity; Inspiring others to believe in abundance

Life direction: Your curriculum is learning that real authority comes from embodying what you teach. You're learning to build wealth, not just talk about it.
</card_meaning>

<source_text>
Allen R. Davis was an American professional football executive and coach. He was the managing general partner, principal owner and de facto general manager for the Oakland Raiders of the National Football League (NFL) for 39 years, from 1972 until his death in 2011. Prior to becoming principal owner of the Raiders, he served as the team's head coach from 1963 to 1965 and as a part-owner from 1966 to 1971, assuming both positions while the Raiders were members of the American Football League (AFL). He served as the AFL commissioner in 1966.
</source_text>

<card_meaning symbol="6♦">
The Generous Provider

You move resources toward other people without erasing your own claim. You naturally want to provide for others. Your resources flow toward helping and supporting. You're the one people come to when they need something.

Balanced: You move resources toward other people without erasing your own claim.

Under-expressed: You over-give and do not say what you need back. Generosity becomes a way to stay unpaid.

Over-expressed: Gifts come with a string. Help becomes a way to keep someone obligated.

Shadow: You keep providing after you are empty. People learn to lean; you learn to resent the lean.

Gifts: Generous and supportive nature with resources; Ability to provide stability for others; Natural understanding of needs and provision; Gift for creating material safety

Life direction: Your curriculum is learning that true generosity includes boundaries. You're learning to give from overflow, not sacrifice.
</card_meaning>

<source_text>
Alan Cedric Page is an American former Minnesota Supreme Court judge and professional football player. After playing college football at the University of Notre Dame, Page gained national recognition as a defensive tackle in the National Football League (NFL) during 15 seasons with the Minnesota Vikings and Chicago Bears. Following his retirement, he then embarked on a legal career. Page earned a B.A. in political science from the University of Notre Dame in 1967 and a J.D. from the University of Minnesota Law School in 1978. Page served as an associate justice of the Minnesota Supreme Court from 1993 until he reached the court's mandatory retirement age of 70 in 2015.
</source_text>

name: Alex Wojciechowicz
slug: alex-wojciechowicz
birth_date: 1915-08-12
birth_card: A♦

<card_meaning symbol="A♦">
The Wealth Pioneer

You start a resource in motion because you trust you can make and keep value. You're wired to build, accumulate, and create resources. Money and material success are your native language. You're the one who starts from nothing and builds something.

Balanced: You start a resource in motion because you trust you can make and keep value.

Under-expressed: You cling to what you have and rehearse losing it. Security work never quite starts.

Over-expressed: You collect to prove you are worth something. Other people start to look like competition.

Shadow: You measure yourself by the pile. More never registers as enough, so success still feels like a shortfall.

Gifts: Natural resource building and accumulation; Ability to see material opportunity; Entrepreneurial drive and initiative; Capacity to create wealth from ideas

Life direction: Your curriculum is learning that worth is not tied to wealth. You're learning that you're enough regardless of what you accumulate.
</card_meaning>

<source_text>
Alexander Francis "Wojie" Wojciechowicz was an American professional football player in the National Football League (NFL) from 1935 to 1950. He was a two-way player who played at center on offense and at linebacker on defense. He has been inducted into both the College and Pro Football Hall of Fame, was a founder and the first president of the NFL Alumni Association, and was the third player to receive the Order of the Leather Helmet.

birth_card: 4♥

<card_meaning symbol="4♥">
The Emotional Foundation Builder

You build a home people can count on, and you leave enough air for feeling to move. You build security in love through consistency, reliability, and trust. You're the steady one—the person others can count on to show up the same way tomorrow. You create the stable home base a relationship needs.

Balanced: You build a home people can count on, and you leave enough air for feeling to move.

Under-expressed: You treat control as safety. Everyone gets a role; nothing unscripted is allowed in.

Over-expressed: You call real emotion messy and shut it down. The house is orderly. Nobody actually lives there.

Shadow: You keep feeling inside approved roles. The house is stable and nothing unscripted is allowed to live there.

Gifts: Building reliable emotional foundations and trust; Consistency and steadiness in relationships; Ability to make others feel safe and held; Loyalty and follow-through in love

Life direction: Your curriculum is learning that a living relationship is unpredictable by nature. You're learning that safety and aliveness aren't opposites.
</card_meaning>

<source_text>
Andre Bernard Tippett Sr. is an American former professional football player who was a linebacker in the National Football League (NFL) for 11 seasons with the New England Patriots. He played college football for the Iowa Hawkeyes, where he was recognized as a consensus All-American in 1981. A second-round pick in the 1982 NFL draft, Tippett was selected to five Pro Bowls and was named first-team All-Pro twice in his career. Since 2007, he has been the Patriots' executive director of community affairs. He was enshrined in the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2008.
</source_text>

<card_meaning symbol="Q♣">
The Nurturing Leader

You teach from what you actually know, without making people earn the right to hear it. You have wisdom, understanding, and the natural ability to mentor. You create intellectual safety where people can grow. You're the wise guide.

Balanced: You teach from what you actually know, without making people earn the right to hear it.

Under-expressed: You know more than you say. Deference keeps the room comfortable and keeps your mind hidden.

Over-expressed: You decide when others are ready. Knowledge becomes a gate you keep.

Shadow: You decide what other people need to understand. Mentorship starts doing their thinking for them.

Gifts: Deep wisdom and thoughtful guidance; Ability to create intellectual safety for growth; Natural mentoring and empowering ability; Talent for helping others develop their thinking

Life direction: Your curriculum is learning that true mentorship means stepping back, letting others struggle and discover. You're learning to trust others' intellectual development.
</card_meaning>

<card_meaning symbol="7♣">
The Analytical Creator

You take a claim apart until the usable piece is left, then you use it. Your mind is sharp, questioning, skeptical. You see through illusions and can identify patterns others miss. You're the critical thinker.

Balanced: You take a claim apart until the usable piece is left, then you use it.

Under-expressed: Skepticism turns into isolation. Nothing is solid enough to act on, so you stay out.

Over-expressed: You complicate the problem past the point of action. Complexity protects you from shipping.

Shadow: You can name every flaw in a plan, so the plan never leaves the table. Analysis does the job of a decision.

Gifts: Penetrating analysis and pattern recognition; Ability to see through surface explanations; Critical thinking and intellectual honesty; Natural skepticism that prevents self-deception

Life direction: Your curriculum is learning that perfect thinking doesn't exist. You're learning to act despite uncertainty, to trust process over perfect analysis.
</card_meaning>

<card_meaning symbol="6♠">
The Responsible Mind

You use what you have already walked through without requiring anyone else to be in pain for it to count. You feel responsibility for helping others think clearly. You're the teacher, the counselor, the one people ask for perspective. Your mind is oriented toward truth and guidance.

Balanced: You use what you have already walked through without requiring anyone else to be in pain for it to count.

Under-expressed: You tend other people's damage and skip your own. Service is how you avoid the wound.

Over-expressed: You need someone to be struggling so your help has a job. Care starts to depend on their not-being-well.

Shadow: You take responsibility for other people seeing it your way. Guidance crowds out their own work.

Gifts: Natural ability to help others see truth; Responsibility toward honest guidance; Clear thinking and balanced perspective; Talent for helping others process difficulty

Life direction: Your curriculum is learning that real guidance means stepping back. You're learning to help without controlling.
</card_meaning>

<source_text>
Arnold Charles "Flash" Herber was an American professional football player who was a quarterback in the National Football League (NFL) for 13 seasons, primarily with the Green Bay Packers. During his Packers tenure from 1930 to 1940, he led the league in passing yards and touchdowns three times and won four NFL Championship Games. Herber retired after 11 seasons in Green Bay, but returned in 1944 with New York Giants, where he played his final two seasons. He was inducted to the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1966.
</source_text>

<card_meaning symbol="Joker">
The Joker: The December 31 Birth Card

December 31 is the only birthday in the year that does not map to one of the 52 cards. The formula resolves it to zero, and zero is the Joker — the card outside the deck's ordered sequence.

Every date runs through the same formula: Solar Value = 55 − (2 × Month + Day). For December 31 that is 55 − (2 × 12 + 31) = 55 − 55 = 0. The cards occupy values 1 through 52, so zero has nowhere to land in the standard deck. December 30 gives 55 − (24 + 30) = 1, the Ace of Hearts — the first card in the sequence. One day later the value steps down again, and there is nothing below the Ace. That is the edge of the system.

In a common year, 364 dates map to one of the 52 cards and December 31 resolves to the Joker. A leap year adds February 29, which maps normally to the 9 of Clubs. We state both edge cases plainly — the system is more useful when the public explanation matches the calculator.

It means the standard card structure does not describe you, and we are not going to pretend otherwise. The 52-card material — birth card, ruling card, life spread positions, compatibility by position — is all built on values 1 through 52. None of it resolves for a value of zero.
</card_meaning>

<card_meaning symbol="Joker">
The Joker: The December 31 Birth Card

December 31 is the only birthday in the year that does not map to one of the 52 cards. The formula resolves it to zero, and zero is the Joker — the card outside the deck's ordered sequence.

Every date runs through the same formula: Solar Value = 55 − (2 × Month + Day). For December 31 that is 55 − (2 × 12 + 31) = 55 − 55 = 0. The cards occupy values 1 through 52, so zero has nowhere to land in the standard deck. December 30 gives 55 − (24 + 30) = 1, the Ace of Hearts — the first card in the sequence. One day later the value steps down again, and there is nothing below the Ace. That is the edge of the system.

In a common year, 364 dates map to one of the 52 cards and December 31 resolves to the Joker. A leap year adds February 29, which maps normally to the 9 of Clubs. We state both edge cases plainly — the system is more useful when the public explanation matches the calculator.

It means the standard card structure does not describe you, and we are not going to pretend otherwise. The 52-card material — birth card, ruling card, life spread positions, compatibility by position — is all built on values 1 through 52. None of it resolves for a value of zero.
</card_meaning>

<source_text>
Richard Paul Kiley was an American stage, film, and television actor and singer. He is best known for his distinguished theatrical career in which he twice won the Tony Award for Best Actor in a Musical. Kiley originated the role of Don Quixote in the original 1965 production of the Broadway musical Man of La Mancha and was the first to sing and record "The Impossible Dream", the hit song from the show. In the 1953 hit musical Kismet, he played the Caliph in the original Broadway cast and as such was one of the quartet who sang "And This Is My Beloved". He also won four Emmy Awards and two Golden Globe Awards during his five-decade career and his "sonorous baritone" was also featured in the narration of a number of documentaries and other films. At the time of his death, Kiley was described as "one of theater's most distinguished and versatile actors" and as "an indispensable actor, the kind of performer who could be called on to play kings and commoners and a diversity of characters in between."
</source_text>

Aaron Copland was an American composer, critic, writer, teacher, pianist, and conductor of his own and other American music. Copland was referred to by his peers and critics as the "Dean of American Music". The open, slowly changing harmonies in much of his music are typical of what many consider the sound of American music, evoking the vast American landscape and pioneer spirit. He is best known for the works he wrote in the 1930s and 1940s in a deliberately accessible style often referred to as "populist" and which he called his "vernacular" style. Works in this vein include the ballets Appalachian Spring, Billy the Kid and Rodeo, his Fanfare for the Common Man and Third Symphony. In addition to his ballets and orchestral works, he produced music in many other genres, including chamber music, vocal works, opera, and film scores.

<card_meaning symbol="Joker">
The Joker: The December 31 Birth Card

December 31 is the only birthday in the year that does not map to one of the 52 cards. The formula resolves it to zero, and zero is the Joker — the card outside the deck's ordered sequence.

Every date runs through the same formula: Solar Value = 55 − (2 × Month + Day). For December 31 that is 55 − (2 × 12 + 31) = 55 − 55 = 0. The cards occupy values 1 through 52, so zero has nowhere to land in the standard deck. December 30 gives 55 − (24 + 30) = 1, the Ace of Hearts — the first card in the sequence. One day later the value steps down again, and there is nothing below the Ace. That is the edge of the system.

In a common year, 364 dates map to one of the 52 cards and December 31 resolves to the Joker. A leap year adds February 29, which maps normally to the 9 of Clubs. We state both edge cases plainly — the system is more useful when the public explanation matches the calculator.

It means the standard card structure does not describe you, and we are not going to pretend otherwise. The 52-card material — birth card, ruling card, life spread positions, compatibility by position — is all built on values 1 through 52. None of it resolves for a value of zero.
</card_meaning>

Ivan Sergeyevich Yarygin was a Soviet and Russian heavyweight freestyle wrestler. Between 1970 and 1980 he won all his major international competitions, except for the 1970 and 1974 European championships where he placed second. After retiring in 1980, he headed the Soviet freestyle wrestling team from 1982 to 1992 and the Russian Wrestling Federation from 1993 until his untimely death in a car crash in 1997. An exceptional upper-body wrestler, Yarygin was widely regarded for his tremendous physique and high-strength aggressive style, always aiming to pin down his opponents, with most of his stoppage wins came by way of fall achieved through rapid fireman's lift and slamming the opponent to the mat. One of the most prestigious tournaments in the World was put together in his honor - The Golden Grand Prix Ivan Yarygin Tournament is held annually in Krasnoyarsk, Russia, and has the reputation of being one of the hardest tournaments in the World. The Yarygin Memorial annually sees the world's best wrestlers come to Siberia, with the added element that Russia's autonomous oblasts and republics such as Dagestan and Chechnya field independent teams alongside an All-Russia selection.
